html:
The Pima, who call themselves Akimel O'odham, "river people", are a Native American people of the Gila and Salt rivers in southern Arizona and of northern Sonora. They speak a Uto-Aztecan language shared with the Tohono O'odham.

They farmed along the rivers with canals, and they see the Hohokam, the great canal builders who lived there before them, as their ancestors. Spanish called their land the Pimería Alta. The Jesuit Eusebio Kino founded missions among them from 1687 and brought wheat and cattle. In 1751 the Pima rose against Spanish rule but were defeated.

In the 1800s the Pima sold wheat to travellers heading for the California Gold Rush and fought beside Americans against the Apache. Upstream dams and settlers then took much of their water, and their farms failed. Today most live in the Gila River and Salt River communities. See also Akimel O'odham on the modern map.
